article.scope_note: This article covers instruments and measurement methods whose main job is to measure the thermal conductivity of the regolith or soil. Payload 009 (heat-flow probe) is referred to only where the two depend on each other; single-point subsurface temperature sensors are payload 011.
article.overview:
The Moon loses heat from its interior, and the rate of loss depends on how the near-surface material conducts heat. A heat-flow measurement therefore needs two quantities: the temperature gradient with depth, and the thermal conductivity of the material it passes through. Conductivity is the quantity that a thermal conductivity probe measures.

Lunar regolith conducts heat very poorly. In the Apollo 15 and 17 analysis, the top few centimetres had a conductivity of about 0.5 to 1.6 mW m⁻¹ K⁻¹ [1]. Apollo 15 and 17 measured conductivity in place by heating a probe and recording how its temperature rose [1][2]. In the sources consulted, these are the only heater-activated in-situ conductivity measurements made on the Moon.

On Mars, the Phoenix Thermal and Electrical Conductivity Probe (TECP) measured soil properties in 2008 using needles pushed into the ground [5][6]. The InSight Heat Flow and Physical Properties Package (HP3) used a self-hammering "mole" as a modified line heat source. Its 2021 conductivity measurement at 0.03–0.37 m depth gave 0.039 ± 0.002 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ [3][4]. Laboratory needle probes and a proposed planetary-scale needle probe are also covered, to show the methods and their limits.
article.description:
A thermal conductivity probe is an instrument that is pushed into the regolith. It has a heater and one or more temperature sensors. A known amount of heat is supplied, and the temperature response is recorded over time. The response depends on how quickly heat spreads into the surrounding material, so its shape gives the conductivity.

Two designs appear in the sources. In the first, a single heated probe acts as a "line heat source", a long thin heater whose temperature rise is analysed as a line-source problem. The Apollo probes, the HP3 mole and the laboratory needle probes all use this principle [1][2][3]. In the second, a set of needles has some elements that heat and others that sense. The Phoenix TECP is an example, and it can also measure electrical properties [5].

In the Apollo and HP3 instruments, conductivity is measured alongside the temperature sensors that give the gradient [1][3].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The main purpose is to supply the conductivity needed to calculate heat flow. Without a measured conductivity, a temperature gradient cannot be converted into heat flux, so conductivity is part of the heat-flow budget as well as an independent planetary property [1][3].

Conductivity also constrains how heat moves through the top metres of soil. HP3 planned to determine thermal diffusivity from the attenuation of the annual temperature wave with depth, and to use conductivity measurements at several depths to build a profile [3]. Surface and near-surface values matter for thermal models of equipment that sits on or in the regolith.

For engineering, the same quantity controls how quickly heat leaves or enters the ground. Apollo's analysis noted that the deeper regolith conductivity was considerably higher than laboratory compaction of lunar soils can explain, which suggests that the soil below a few centimetres has been compacted by natural processes [1].
article.operating_principle:
A line heat source is a long heater in a material. Let Q be the heating power per unit length. For an infinite cylinder in an infinite, homogeneous medium, the temperature rise at a fixed sensor location after many time constants follows a simple form. The temperature rise is proportional to the natural logarithm of time, and the proportionality constant is set by Q and the conductivity k [1][2].

In the Apollo report, the slope of the temperature rise against ln(t) is written as a constant c₁ = −Q/(4πk), where Q is the power per unit length [1]. The HP3 paper uses the same idea and writes the heating curve as T = C₁ ln(t) + C₂, with the conductivity given by k = q/(4π C₁) [3]. Here q is heating power per unit length, and for the HP3 mole q = RI²/l_Mole [3].

Two practical points follow from these equations. First, the logarithmic form is only reliable after the probe has heated the surrounding ground for long enough. Langseth's model was used for times greater than 20 h [1]. Second, the result depends on how much heat is lost axially along the probe and into the probe's support structure. Langseth identified this as the main source of error in the Apollo determinations [1].

For needle probes, the Nagihara et al. paper describes a standard reduction that plots temperature against ln(t) and takes the slope. It also proposes a modified reduction based on the exact solution for a finite-length line source [2].
article.scientific_importance:
Conductivity is the link between measured temperature gradients and the heat that leaves the Moon. Apollo's conductivity results, combined with temperature gradients, gave heat-flow estimates at two sites [1]. The heat-flow probe article (payload 009) gives the associated site values.

Conductivity measurements also test models of regolith physics. Low surface values of 0.5 to 1.6 mW m⁻¹ K⁻¹ indicate a fine, low-density top layer [1]. The deeper, compacted layer conducts more heat, and Apollo's authors used this to argue for natural compaction below a few centimetres [1].

On Mars, the HP3 result of 0.039 ± 0.002 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 0.03–0.37 m depth provides a measured soil conductivity from a flown instrument at a second planetary surface [4]. Together with the Phoenix TECP mission, it shows how conductivity probes are used beyond the Apollo era, although the two Mars instruments differ in design and in what they report.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power for a thermal conductivity probe. The designs below use different heaters, geometries and sensors, and the data are not directly comparable. Values are given only for the named instrument and source. Where a value is not stated in the sources read, the article says so.

examples.name: Apollo 15 and 17 Heat Flow Experiment conductivity measurements
examples.status: Flown on the Moon at the Apollo 15 and Apollo 17 sites.
examples.probe_design: Heaters surrounding each gradient-sensor housing, energised at 0.002 W or 0.5 W; only the lower power was used at both sites, because the inferred conductivities were low [1]. Nagihara et al. describe the Apollo probe as 2.5 cm in diameter and heated for 40 hours [2].
examples.measurement_method: Heaters energised in sequence for periods of 36 hours or more; measurements made in the first 60 days after deployment, when sensors were free of large diurnal variations [1]. Conductivity determined by comparing observed slopes on a logarithmic time scale with values calculated from finite-difference models [1].

thermal_conductivity.surface_layer: About 2–3 cm thick; about 0.5 to 1.6 mW m⁻¹ K⁻¹ [1].
thermal_conductivity.below_10_cm: 10 mW m⁻¹ K⁻¹ ±10% (Apollo 15); 15 mW m⁻¹ K⁻¹ ±10% (Apollo 17) [1].
thermal_conductivity.methods_note: Deeper values were partly derived from the downward propagation of long-period temperature changes, not from heater tests alone [1]. Values read from OCR of the 1977 report.

examples.mass_and_dimensions: Probe mass and dimensions not stated in the sources read.

examples.name: InSight HP3 mole conductivity measurement (Mars)
examples.type: Flown Mars instrument (self-penetrating mole used as a modified line heat source)
examples.status: Flown on the InSight lander, Mars (from 2018). Conductivity result published in 2021 [4].
examples.probe_design: Mole about 400 mm long and 27 mm in diameter. Carries the Science Tether with 14 platinum resistance temperature sensors (PT100) [3]. TEM-A heater foils: Kapton-based copper heaters glued to the outer casing and protected by aluminium covers; the copper resistance also gives temperature. Heating power between 0 and 2 W [3].
examples.measurement_method: Modified line heat source. Heating curve T = C1 ln(t) + C2; conductivity k = q/(4π C1), with q = RI²/l_Mole [3]. Planned heating duration 24 hours with a target TEM-A temperature rise of 10 K [3].

thermal_conductivity.error_budget: Conductivity term 2.6% in the heat-flow error budget for a nominal conductivity of 0.05 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ [3].
thermal_conductivity.measured_result: Average soil conductivity of 0.039 ± 0.002 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ over 0.03–0.37 m depth, after emplacing the probe to a 0.37 m tip depth [4]. Read from the abstract only.

examples.mass_and_dimensions: Mole about 400 mm long and 27 mm in diameter [3]. Mole mass not stated in the sources read.
examples.monitoring_span: Not stated for conductivity; the later monitoring phase uses hourly temperature measurements [3].

examples.name: Laboratory needle probes (engineering tests; not flown)
examples.type: Engineering models and laboratory test instruments
examples.status: Not flight hardware. Tests in a laboratory vacuum chamber on JSC-1A lunar simulant [2].
examples.probe_design: Decagon TR-1 commercial needle probe: stainless steel casing 2.4 mm outside diameter and 10 cm long, with heater wire and a thermistor at its centre. KS-1 needle probe: 1.3 mm diameter [2].
examples.measurement_method: Line-heat-source needle method; two data-reduction schemes compared (standard slope method and a proposed exact-solution method) [2].
examples.test_conditions: JSC-1A lunar simulant compacted by vibration in a container of about 3 litres; pressure 0.13 Pa (1 mTorr) to 101 kPa (760 Torr); room temperature [2].
examples.reported_agreement: TR-1 and KS-1 agreed within 0.8% at 0.27 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ at atmospheric pressure. Both schemes agreed within 3% above 1000 Pa. The standard reduction overestimated conductivity by 100–150% below 100 Pa [2].
examples.requirement_stated: Conductivity measurable to better than 0.01 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ [2].
examples.mass_and_dimensions: TR-1 casing 2.4 mm outside diameter and 10 cm length [2]. Instrument mass not stated.

examples.name: Proposed planetary-scale needle probe (concept; not flown)
examples.status: Proposed; no flight unit described in the sources read.
examples.probe_design: Proposed needle probes of greater diameter (1 to 2.5 cm) and length (30 to 50 cm) than laboratory probes, for use in planetary regolith [2].
examples.measurement_method: Proposed data-reduction algorithm based on the exact solution for the probe; claimed to shorten measurement time on planetary surfaces by an order of magnitude. Not validated on lunar regolith in the sources read [2].

thermal_conductivity.note: No measured values for this concept.

examples.mass_and_dimensions: Diameter 1 to 2.5 cm; length 30 to 50 cm (proposed) [2]. Mass not stated.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are given per example and are not comparable across designs. Apollo probe diameter 2.5 cm as cited by Nagihara et al. [2]; Apollo probe length not stated in the sources read. TECP needles 15 mm long [6]; needle diameter not stated. HP3 mole about 400 mm long and 27 mm in diameter [3]. Laboratory TR-1 casing 2.4 mm outside diameter and 10 cm long [2]. Proposed planetary-scale probe 1 to 2.5 cm in diameter and 30 to 50 cm long [2] (concept only).
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is not stated for any flown example in the sources read, including the HP3 mole [3] and the Apollo probes [1]. Laboratory and proposed mass values are not stated. No universal mass is implied for a thermal conductivity probe.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Apollo: heater setting 0.002 W for the low mode used at both sites [1]. HP3: TEM-A heater foils supply 0 to 2 W [3]. TECP: heater power not stated in the sources read. Laboratory probes and proposed concept: not stated.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
Conductivity measurements depend on the surrounding environment and on the time allowed for the ground to settle. Lunar regolith is in vacuum, and laboratory tests showed that pressure changes the measured result. The standard reduction overestimated conductivity by 100–150% below 100 Pa [2].

Thermal settling is required before measurement. Apollo heating was done in the first 60 days after deployment, when the sensors were free of large diurnal variations [1]. HP3 required a cooldown of at least 48 hours after hammering before its conductivity measurement [3].

Heater power must be low enough not to disturb the regolith being measured. HP3 set a target temperature rise of 10 K, chosen to give a good signal-to-noise ratio without significantly affecting the regolith conductivity [3].
article.limitations:
The Apollo heater analysis depends on modelled thermal properties of the probe and its support, because they control how much heat flows axially along the probe. Langseth identified these assumptions as the main source of error in the heater-activated determinations [1].

Apollo's deeper conductivity values were partly derived from long-period temperature waves, not only from heater tests. The result therefore depends on the model used for those waves [1].

Measured values for the Moon are limited. The sources read describe Apollo's heater results and a laboratory simulant. They do not describe a modern lunar conductivity probe, and the Apollo results are not for a new instrument.

For HP3, the 2021 result is a single measurement reported in the abstract, at one depth range. A full depth profile depended on further hammering and additional measurements. Those results were not read in full [3][4].

Laboratory results depend on probe-to-material contact and on simulant. The 2013 comparisons were made on JSC-1A simulant, not lunar regolith [2].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A thermal conductivity probe may be delivered to the Moon as a dedicated instrument, or as part of a heat-flow package with a temperature sensor string. Transport and deployment requirements depend strongly on the design.
transportation_process: Integrate the probe into the spacecraft or lander payload compartment on Earth.
Launch and transfer to the Moon.
Deliver to the surface by a lunar lander, then deploy the probe into the regolith (by astronaut or robotic mechanism, depending on design).
Power the heater and sensors; heat for the planned period (Apollo: 36 hours or more per heating) and allow the ground to settle before each measurement.
Record temperature response and downlink data for analysis. Compatibility with any specific lander is not assessed here.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo probes were placed by astronauts in drilled holes [7]. HP3 mole was hammered into the soil and paused at stops to make conductivity measurements at about 50 cm intervals, with a cooldown of at least 48 hours before each measurement [3]. TECP's needles were inserted into the soil [6]; the insertion mechanism is not described in the sources read.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 15 and 17 heater-activated measurements on the Moon [1]; Phoenix TECP (2008) [5][6]; InSight HP3 mole (2018 onward; conductivity 2021) [3][4].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lunar lander, rover or spacecraft has been assessed for compatibility with a conductivity probe. Mass, dimensions, mounting, deployment loads, power and data interfaces would need to be compared with verified lander specifications before any assignment is made.

article.historical_significance:
Apollo 15 and 17 made the first heater-activated in-situ measurements of lunar regolith conductivity in the sources consulted [1][2]. Their values underpin lunar heat-flow estimates [1].

The Phoenix TECP measured soil thermal properties on Mars in 2008 with needles inserted into the soil [5][6]. InSight's HP3 mole measured soil conductivity on Mars at a depth of 0.03–0.37 m [4]. These flown Martian measurements are in a different environment from the Moon, and their results should not be used as lunar values.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- **Apollo conductivity values.** The values come from OCR of the 1977 final report, which is noisy. The surface-layer range and deeper values should be checked against the scanned page before reuse [1]. The probe mass and dimensions are not stated in the sources read. A heater length of 1.7 cm mentioned in a secondary summary was not found in the report text and is not used.
- **Apollo timing.** Heating periods are reported as 36 hours or more [1] and as 40 hours [2]. Both are of the same order, but the sources do not describe the same test sequence.
- **PDS bundle wording.** The Apollo 15 PDS bundle describes temperature readings, while its summary refers to thermal conductivity measurements [7]. The archived products were not inspected.
- **Phoenix TECP.** The Zent et al. (2009) paper returned HTTP 404 and was not read. Needle diameter, conductivity range and accuracy, duration, mass and power are not verified.
- **HP3 mole.** The Spohn et al. (2018) paper was read in full. The Grott et al. (2021) result was read from its abstract only. The test date, the full uncertainty analysis and the mole's mass are not verified. The heater-foil geometry is taken from the 2018 design description, which may differ from the flight unit.
- **Laboratory probes.** The Nagihara et al. manuscript is a 2013 draft. The published journal version was not checked. The TR-1 and KS-1 probes are commercial and laboratory devices, not flight instruments.
- **Proposed planetary-scale probe.** The 1–2.5 cm diameter, 30–50 cm length, and the claimed order-of-magnitude reduction in measurement time are proposals. They are not validated on lunar regolith in the sources read.
- **Cone-tip prototype.** A NASA cone-tip heat-flow probe with an in-situ conductivity probe was identified (NTRS 20140010048), but its PDF returned no readable text. It is not described in this article.
- **Japanese prototype.** A 2014 JpGU conference abstract on a conductivity probe returned HTTP 403 and was not read.
- **Images.** The TECP image (PIA11722) and the HP3 mole image (PIA24263) are Mars images. Neither shows the conductivity sensing elements in detail. No verified photograph of a lunar conductivity probe was identified.
- **Scope.** This article does not give lunar landing-site recommendations. Those are deferred by the user.

data_quality_notes: Scope: stand-alone thermal conductivity measurement methods and instruments. Heat-flow probes (payload 009) and single-point subsurface temperature sensors (payload 011) are excluded except where conductivity depends on them.

Apollo 15 and 17 conductivity values (surface 0.5 to 1.6 mW/m K; deeper 10 and 15 mW/m K with ±10%) come from OCR of the 1977 final report and should be checked against the scanned page before reuse. The same values are used in payload 009.

Apollo heater details: heater power 0.002 W (low mode) and heating periods of 36 hours or more are from the 1977 report. The Nagihara et al. manuscript describes the Apollo probe as 2.5 cm in diameter and heated for 40 hours. The sources do not describe the same test sequence.
Unverified claim: a heater length of 1.7 cm appeared in a secondary search summary. It was not found in the report text and is not used.
Apollo probe mass, dimensions and length are not stated in the sources read.
PDS Apollo 15 HFE bundle: description refers to temperature readings, while the Primary_Result_Summary refers to reduced thermal conductivity measurements. Data product members were not inspected.

Phoenix TECP: Zent et al. (2009) JGR paper returned HTTP 404 and was not read. Needle diameter, conductivity range and accuracy, measurement duration, mass and power are not verified. The WUSTL page does not name the heat-pulse technique; the method is described as the heating and cooling behaviour of the needles.

HP3 mole: the Spohn et al. (2018) paper was read in full from the saved DLR PDF. Mole mass, the full HP3 mass and power, and the flight-unit heater geometry are not verified. The 2018 design description may differ from the flight unit.
HP3 conductivity result: Grott et al. (2021) read from its abstract only. Test date, sol and detailed uncertainty budget are not verified. The e-docs.geo-leo.de copy returned HTTP 403.

Laboratory needle probe results: NTRS 20140010297 is a 2013 manuscript draft; the published journal version was not checked. The TR-1 and KS-1 probes are commercial and laboratory devices, not flight instruments.

Proposed planetary-scale needle probe: diameter 1 to 2.5 cm, length 30 to 50 cm, and the order-of-magnitude reduction in measurement time are proposals, not validated on lunar regolith in the sources read.

Not read: NASA NTRS 20140010048 (cone-tip heat-flow probe prototype) returned a PDF with no readable text in the first 39,912 of 227,056 characters; excluded from the article. JpGU 2014 abstract PPS26-P01 (Japanese conductivity probe prototype) returned HTTP 403; excluded.

Images: PIA11722 (TECP, Mars) and PIA24263 (HP3 mole, Mars) are verified as direct JPEG assets. Neither shows the internal heater or sensing elements in detail. No verified photograph of a lunar conductivity probe was found.
